title: Why Your Brain Deletes Most of What You See
summary: Your eyes take in far more information than your conscious mind ever processes. This Short explains the attentional bottleneck and change blindness in under 30 seconds.
hook: You just missed something huge... and your brain is the reason.
narration: Right now your eyes are taking in millions of bits of information. But your conscious mind only processes a tiny fraction. Scientists call this the attentional bottleneck. In classic change-blindness experiments, people fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through a scene. Your brain is not a camera. It is a ruthless editor. It keeps what it thinks matters and throws the rest away. That is why you can look straight at something and still not see it.

title: The Number That Breaks Infinity
summary: Hilbert’s Hotel shows how infinity can still have empty rooms even when every room is full. A clean visual explanation of countable infinity.
hook: A hotel with infinite rooms is completely full... yet it still has space for more guests.
narration: Imagine a hotel with infinitely many rooms, and every single room is occupied. A new guest arrives. Is the hotel full? Not quite. The manager asks the guest in room 1 to move to room 2, the guest in room 2 to move to room 3, and so on. Suddenly room 1 is free. This is Hilbert’s Hotel, a thought experiment that shows countable infinity can still absorb more. Infinity is not a number. It is a different kind of size.

title: Why Time Moves Slower When You Move Faster
summary: Special relativity time dilation explained in plain language with a clear visual of clocks running at different rates.
hook: The faster you move, the slower time passes for you. This is not science fiction.
narration: According to Einstein’s special relativity, time is not absolute. If you travel close to the speed of light, your clock runs slower compared to someone standing still. This is called time dilation. GPS satellites have to correct for it every day or their positioning would drift. The effect is tiny at everyday speeds, but it is real, measured, and built into the technology you use.
